title: Landlord Security Responsibilities in California: What You're Liable For (and What You're Not)

findings.quote: The liability window opens when a tenant reports a broken lock. Fix it fast and log it.
findings.root_cause: The summary, takeaway, coverage bullet, metadata and script frame notice as tenant-report-only and blur statutory violation with liability for crime. Section 1941.3(b) also covers actual knowledge. Source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1941.3.
findings.fix: Replace the takeaway and script notice opening with: 'Once you know a required lock is defective—whether through a tenant report or your own observation—act promptly and document the repair. Notice alone does not establish liability for a later crime.' Replace the summary’s tenant-notice sentences with: 'Under Civil Code §1941.3(b), a landlord can be liable for a violation if a covered defect remains uncorrected beyond a reasonable time after the landlord or agent actually knows about it or receives notice. A tenant report is one way to establish notice. Liability for injuries from a crime also requires the other elements of the claim, including causation.' Replace the coverage bullet with: 'Why actual knowledge or a report of a defective required lock calls for prompt action.' Replace the meta-description with: 'California landlord security duties: required locks, responding to known defects, and how foreseeability affects potential liability for crime.'
findings.future_prevention: Check the short answer, tables, FAQs, metadata and both copies of the video script against the same qualified rule before recording or publishing.

findings.quote: California law requires a working deadbolt on each main entry door, locks on windows that open, and locking exterior doors into common areas of multifamily buildings.
findings.root_cause: The standalone page and script omit the statute’s covered-door/window qualifications. Readers of this asset do not receive the blog’s later exception list.
findings.fix: Replace the summary’s first sentence and script lock list with: 'Subject to statutory exceptions, Civil Code §1941.3 requires deadbolts on main swinging unit-entry doors, security or locking devices on covered openable windows, and code-compliant locks on exterior common-area doors with access to units in multifamily buildings.' Add after the summary: 'The full guide explains the sliding-door, window, existing-hardware and other statutory exceptions.'
findings.future_prevention: Check the short answer, tables, FAQs, metadata and both copies of the video script against the same qualified rule before recording or publishing.

findings.quote: Are you liable when a tenant is the victim of a crime at your rental? In California, usually not, but a few things change that answer fast.
findings.root_cause: The hook generalizes the outcome of fact-specific negligence claims. 'General neighborhood crime usually doesn’t' also applies the guard-duty discussion too broadly to foreseeability overall. 'Low-cost fixes ... most often get caught' makes an unsupported frequency claim. The protected-tenant takeaway lacks the co-tenant distinction and direct statutory citations.
findings.fix: Replace the opening in the page, excerpt and script with: 'A crime alone does not make a California landlord liable. The questions include what risk was foreseeable, what reasonable precautions were required, and whether a failure contributed to the harm.' Replace the neighborhood/guard sentence with: 'A duty to hire guards generally requires heightened foreseeability, which can come from prior similar incidents or other sufficiently serious warning signs; less burdensome precautions require a separate assessment.' Replace 'Low-cost fixes to known problems are where landlords most often get caught' with 'Address known defects promptly; the burden of a precaution matters when courts assess duty.' Replace the protected-tenant takeaway with: 'A written request with the required documentation can trigger a 24-hour, landlord-paid lock change. Section 1941.6 co-tenant cases require a qualifying court order excluding that person.' Add resource links to https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1941.5. and https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1941.6. and the cited Ann M./Castaneda decisions. Replace 'protect you from liability and help keep good tenants' in the script with 'can help reduce risk and support tenant retention.'
findings.future_prevention: Check the short answer, tables, FAQs, metadata and both copies of the video script against the same qualified rule before recording or publishing.
